title: Time dependence in quantum theory
scope: Secs. 5.1 to 5.6 and 5.8 (Schrodinger, Heisenberg and interaction pictures, linear response time evolution, time-dependent operators, Fermi's golden rule, Fourier transforms of retarded and advanced functions). Excluded: 5.7 (T-matrix and generalized golden rule, Eqs. 5.35-5.41), 5.9 is a summary.

For the first identity, add and subtract $ACB$:
$$[AB,C]=ABC-CAB=ABC-ACB+ACB-CAB=A[B,C]+[A,C]B.$$
For the second, add and subtract $ACB$ with the other sign:
$$[AB,C]=ABC-CAB=ABC+ACB-ACB-CAB=A\{B,C\}-\{A,C\}B.$$
The first form suits bosons and the second suits fermions.

questions.prompt: Fermi's golden rule for the transition rate between $|i\rangle$ and $|f\rangle$ is
questions.solution: Eq. (5.34) with $\hbar=1$. The rate is quadratic in the matrix element, and the delta function enforces energy conservation.

questions.prompt: What does the interaction picture split off, and why is it useful for perturbation theory?
questions.solution:
The interaction picture moves the trivial $H_0$ evolution into the operators, $\hat A(t)=e^{iH_0t}Ae^{-iH_0t}$. The states then evolve only with $\hat V(t)$, through $\hat U(t,t_0)$, Eq. (5.11).

Expanding $\hat U$ in powers of $\hat V$ gives a perturbation series, Eq. (5.18). Each order contains only the interaction, and the free phases are already in the operators.

questions.prompt: Show that the third-order term of $\hat U(t,t_0)$ equals $\frac{(-i)^3}{3!}\int\!\!\int\!\!\int \mathcal T_t[\hat V(t_1)\hat V(t_2)\hat V(t_3)]$ (Book Exercise 5.2).
questions.solution:
Book Exercise 5.2. Iterating $\hat U=1-i\int\hat V\,\hat U$ (Eq. 5.14) gives the ordered term
$$\hat U_3=(-i)^3\int_{t_0}^t dt_1\int_{t_0}^{t_1}dt_2\int_{t_0}^{t_2}dt_3\,\hat V(t_1)\hat V(t_2)\hat V(t_3),$$
where the integration region is $t_1>t_2>t_3$.

The time-ordered product $\mathcal T_t[\hat V(t_1)\hat V(t_2)\hat V(t_3)]$ is the same for every ordering of the three times, once the operators are placed in time order (Eq. 5.17). Over the full cube $[t_0,t]^3$ each of the $3!=6$ orderings contributes the same integral after relabeling. So the ordered integral is $1/3!$ of the unrestricted integral of the time-ordered product.

Hence
$$\hat U_3=\frac{(-i)^3}{3!}\int\!\!\int\!\!\int_{t_0}^t\mathcal T_t[\hat V(t_1)\hat V(t_2)\hat V(t_3)],$$
which is the n = 3 term of the exponential in Eq. (5.18).

questions.prompt: Show that $\int dx\,\frac{f(x)}{x+i\eta}=\mathcal P\!\!\int dx\,\frac{f(x)}{x}-i\pi f(0)$ for $\eta\to0^+$ (Book Exercise 5.7).
questions.solution:
Book Exercise 5.7. Split the denominator into real and imaginary parts:
$$\frac{1}{x+i\eta}=\frac{x}{x^2+\eta^2}-i\frac{\eta}{x^2+\eta^2}.$$
As $\eta\to0^+$, the first term tends to the principal value $\mathcal P(1/x)$ in the distributional sense. The second term is a Lorentzian of width $\eta$ and weight $\pi$, so $\frac{\eta}{x^2+\eta^2}\to\pi\delta(x)$. Therefore
$$\int dx\,\frac{f(x)}{x+i\eta}\to\mathcal P\!\!\int dx\,\frac{f(x)}{x}-i\pi f(0).$$

questions.prompt: For $f^R(t)=-i\theta(t)e^{-i\varepsilon t}$, compute $f^R(\omega)$ with Eq. (5.46) and invert it with Eq. (5.47) (Book Exercise 5.8).
questions.solution:
Book Exercise 5.8. With the convergence factor,
$$f^R(\omega)=\int_0^\infty dt\,e^{i\omega t}e^{-\eta t}(-i)e^{-i\varepsilon t}=-i\int_0^\infty dt\,e^{i(\omega-\varepsilon+i\eta)t}=\frac{1}{\omega-\varepsilon+i\eta},$$
using $\int_0^\infty e^{iat}dt=i/a$ for $\mathrm{Im}\,a>0$.

Inverse transform:
$$f^R(t)=\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}e^{-i\omega t}\frac{1}{\omega-\varepsilon+i\eta}.$$
For $t>0$, close the contour in the lower half plane, where $e^{-i\omega t}$ decays. The only pole is at $\omega=\varepsilon-i\eta$, enclosed clockwise, so
$$f^R(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi}(-2\pi i)\,e^{-i\varepsilon t}e^{-\eta t}\to-i\,e^{-i\varepsilon t}.$$
For $t<0$, close in the upper half plane. There is no pole, so $f^R(t)=0$.
Result: $f^R(t)=-i\theta(t)e^{-i\varepsilon t}$, as required.
